stem: Which statement about the `else` block after a `for` or `while` loop is true?

options.text: It runs only when the loop body never runs
options.rationale: An empty loop does run the `else`, but so does a loop that finishes all its rounds normally.

options.text: It runs only when the loop ends with `break`
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the rule: `break` is what skips the `else` block.

options.text: It runs once each time a round of the loop finishes
options.rationale: The loop's `else` runs at most once, after the whole loop is over.

options.text: It runs once, unless the loop ends with `break`
options.rationale: Think of the loop's `else` as "no break": it runs after a normal finish, even after zero rounds.

explanation: The loop's `else` block runs once, after the loop has finished on its own: when a `while` condition becomes false or a `for` loop runs out of items, including when there were no rounds at all. If the loop is left with `break`, the `else` is skipped.

stem: What is the output of the following code?

options.rationale: `range(1, 6)` stops before 6, so the last value `n` takes is 5.
`continue` skips the rest of a round but does not change `n`; the loop still reaches 5.
`n > 7` is never true, so no `break` happens; `continue` doesn't stop the `else`, which sees the last value, 5.
`continue` only skips to the next round. Without a `break`, the `else` block runs.

explanation: `n` takes the values 1 to 5. Even numbers hit `continue`, which only skips to the next round. `n > 7` is never true, so `break` never runs. The loop finishes normally, the `else` runs, and `n` still holds its last value, 5.

stem: Complete the code so that it stops searching once Dan is found and prints only `Dan is coming`.
code:
guests = ["Ana", "Dan", "Cleo"]
i = 0
while i < len(guests):
    if guests[i] == "Dan":
        print("Dan is coming")
        __BLANK1__
    i += 1
__BLANK2__:
    print("Dan is not on the list")

blanks.rationale: `break` ends the loop at once, which also means its `else` block is skipped.
An `else` lined up with `while` belongs to the loop and runs only if the loop ends without `break`.

explanation: The search stops with `break` when Dan is found. Because the loop ended with `break`, the `else` block lined up with `while` is skipped, so `Dan is not on the list` is not printed. With `pass`, the loop would carry on to the end and the `else` would run as well.

stem: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `Vowel found: o`.
rationale: The word is set first, the `for` loop checks each letter, the message comes before `break`, and the `else` lines up with `for` after the loop body.
explanation: The loop goes through `c`, `r`, `y`, `p` and `t` without finding a vowel. At `o`, it prints `Vowel found: o` and `break` ends the loop. The `else` block belongs to the `for` loop, so it is skipped because of the `break`. If `break` came before `print()`, nothing would be printed.

stem: Which line, inserted at the marked spot, makes the program print only `Too expensive: 25`?

options.rationale: `continue` only skips to the next round. The loop still finishes normally, so the `else` prints `All affordable`.
`break` ends the loop at 25, and a loop left with `break` skips its `else`.
`pass` does nothing, so the loop finishes normally and the `else` still runs.
This prints 25 a second time, and the loop still finishes normally, so the `else` runs too.

explanation: To keep `All affordable` from being printed, the loop must end with `break`: the `else` of a loop runs only when the loop finishes without `break`. `continue` and `pass` don't stop the loop, so the `else` would still run.
